title: Catch-22 and the contradictions of Nepal’s democracy - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Catch-22 and the contradictions of Nepal’s democracy  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Foreign employment workers leaving Nepal.

For many Nepalis, the choice is deceptively simple. They can stay in a country where opportunities to build a decent life remain scarce, or leave in search of work abroad and send money back to support those who remain. This is hardly a choice at all. It reflects a fundamental contradiction in a country that promises its citizens rights, opportunities and prosperity but often fails to provide the conditions necessary to secure them at home.

This contradiction persists despite decades of political change, constitutional promises and successive commitments to reform. From education and employment to healthcare, governance and development, the gap between what the state promises and what citizens experience remains wide. These are not simply policy failures. They point to a deeper institutional cycle in which political actors repeatedly create problems they appear unable or unwilling to resolve.

Joseph Heller’s Catch-22 offers a useful way to understand this predicament. The term describes a self-defeating system of rules in which the conditions for escaping a problem make escape impossible. It captures the absurdity of institutions that manipulate logic and language to protect their authority while leaving ordinary people trapped in contradictions. Nepal’s political and social realities increasingly resemble this predicament.

Nepal’s transition from monarchy to a federal democratic republic was one of South Asia’s most consequential political transformations. Many people paid a heavy price in the struggle to establish an inclusive, participatory society and a new political order. Yet the journey remains uncertain. Political leaders’ commitments repeatedly fall short of meaningful implementation, leaving citizens expected to solve problems that the system itself seems designed to keep unresolved. The result is growing frustration, the normalisation of irrationality and institutions increasingly insulated from public scrutiny.

The bluster of Catch-22

Thirty-six years have passed since democracy was restored in Nepal in 1990. Yet the achievements of that period have been undermined by persistent institutional instability and stagnation. Institutions need stability to mature, but reforms driven by short-term political interests rather than long-term institutional needs repeatedly unsettle them.

The Constitution of Nepal, 2015, sought to establish federalism, inclusiveness and power-sharing. However, its implementation has become entangled in disputes over identity, representation and the distribution of power. Politicians who once appeared committed to structural change have often become defenders of the status quo after acquiring power. This paradox raises serious questions about democratic competition and further weakens the institutions meant to uphold the constitutional order.

The Constitution guarantees social justice, education, healthcare and equality as fundamental rights. These commitments place Nepal among South Asia’s more progressive constitutional democracies. Yet their meaningful realisation remains elusive. Political systems often reward conformity rather than responsiveness to the needs and concerns of ordinary people, allowing the gap between constitutional promises and everyday realities to persist.

The Gen Z uprising sought national renewal. It challenged institutionalised corruption, impunity, political privilege and the established political class. The deadly crackdown claimed 76 lives and left more than 2,000 people injured. But what substantive gains has the country made since then? The uprising risks becoming a nihilistic revolution, one that destroys before it rebuilds.

Michel Foucault argued that modern political power operates not merely through force but also through institutions, knowledge, surveillance and discipline. His work offers a useful perspective on how power is exercised in Nepal today. By failing to deliver the change they were promised, the present government’s actions risk dashing the hopes and expectations of ordinary people, particularly the poor.

What is fuelling Catch-22 in Nepal?

A country’s decline can begin when people come to believe that a single individual can rescue it from crisis and place that individual above the nation and its institutions.

Hitler’s rise in Germany offers a stark historical warning. He was elevated as an indispensable leader who could rescue the country from its crisis. The consequences were catastrophic. As the Nazi regime consolidated power, German soldiers were required to swear personal loyalty to Hitler rather than to the Constitution. Allegiance to an individual had replaced loyalty to the nation and its constitutional order.

A second warning sign emerges when people are persuaded that political opposition amounts to hostility towards the nation. Those who engage in such manipulation seek to poison public discourse and turn citizens against their opponents. Rather than encourage debate and disagreement, they cultivate suspicion and portray dissent as a threat.

The danger deepens when governments and their institutions attempt to control what people hear and suppress public voices. Such practices undermine fundamental rights and leave citizens with little room to challenge authority.

Hannah Arendt, the German-American political thinker, examined how totalitarian systems seek to eliminate independent thought and public dissent, replacing them with unquestioning obedience to authority. Her work offers an important lens through which to understand the dangers of political systems that treat criticism as disloyalty.

Breaking the cycle of Catch-22

Breaking this cycle requires vigilant, questioning and thoughtful citizens who reject the idea that one individual can provide the answer to every national problem. A leader can initiate change and play a catalytic role in bringing it about, but no individual can substitute for strong institutions, accountable government and an engaged citizenry.

First, we must reject the idea of an unchecked leader who can wave a magic wand and lift the country out of crisis. Political authority must remain subject to constitutional limits, institutional oversight and public accountability.

Second, political parties must reform themselves and develop policy-based manifestos that offer credible solutions to national problems. Candidates who deliberately spread falsehoods to manipulate election outcomes or secure sympathy votes should face appropriate legal and political consequences.

Third, an independent judiciary is essential to upholding justice, restoring public confidence and ensuring the rule of law. Without judicial independence, constitutional guarantees risk remaining promises on paper rather than protections in people’s lives.

Ultimately, good governance, democratic values and constitutional supremacy depend not on politicians alone but on citizens who refuse to surrender their rights or accept arbitrary exercises of power.

The answer lies in the political awareness of sovereign citizens. Civic consciousness gives people the confidence to question rulers, challenge arbitrary decisions and demand accountability. Through such vigilance, Nepal can begin to restore its democratic institutions and protect human freedom.

full_article:
Birgunj (Parsa), Nov 7: With the objective of providing services to general people in easy, smooth and accessible manner, the Nepal Telecom has launched a service to deliver SIM cards directly to doorsteps of customers.

The Department of Postal Service and Nepal Telecom have signed agreement in order to deliver SIM cards of the Nepal Telecom to doorsteps of customers inside Parsa district through postal service.

Postal Officer at the District Post Office, Namanath Yadav, shared that they have started providing SIM cards with an objective of providing services to customers to their doorsteps in an easy and smooth manner.

After filling the Nepal Telecom's online form for the SIM card, customers could receive their SIM cards at their address through postal service. With the beginning of the service, employee of post office reached the house of Kiran Kumari Chauhan at Birhunj metropolis-10 and provided the SIM card for the first time. (RSS)

title: Nepal seeks stronger recognition of mountain issues in UN climate process - Climate Home News
description: Nepal seeks stronger recognition of mountain issues in UN climate process  Climate Home News
publisher.title: Climate Home News
full_article:
In the wake of its recent glacial flooding disaster, Nepal and the kingdom of Bhutan have proposed a new agenda item on mountains and climate change for the COP31 summit which opens on Monday in the Turkish city of Antalya.

In a submission addressed to the COP31 presidency and the head of the UN climate secretariat (UNFCCC), Nepal said the agenda item, entitled “1.5°C Warming in Mountains”, is an effort to strengthen the response of the international community to the climate risks facing the world’s mountain regions.

The item proposes that mountain issues should become a regular part of the formal UN climate change process, with a focus on scientific assessment of the risks associated with warming overshooting 1.5C, an annual high-level dialogue, a dedicated work programme and improved access to climate finance.

Maheshwar Dhakal, chief of the climate change management division of Nepal’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment, told Climate Home News that Himalayan countries face similar problems such as collapsing glaciers and flooding from glacial lakes.

“We are trying to bring all Himalayan countries together under this agenda item,” he said.

COP31 Briefing: What to expect from the Antalya climate summit?

At this year’s UN General Assembly, Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah called for strong global action to ensure climate justice and proposed creating a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by India, China and Nepal. It would share satellite data, monitor glacial slopes and lakes, strengthen early warning systems and coordinate cross-border disaster response.

Nepal has experienced significant infrastructure losses and human casualties from flooding every year since 2020. In late August, the collapse of a glacial slope on the border with Tibet caused a torrent of water and debris to course down the Bhote Koshi River, leaving more than 6,000 people dead or missing.

According to a government needs assessment, the disaster caused an estimated $2.7 billion in physical damage and economic losses, while around $4.8 billion will be required for recovery and reconstruction.

More research needed on threats

Although high mountain regions are known to be fragile ecosystems, especially as global warming accelerates glacier melt, the extent of their vulnerability is still not fully understood. When the devastating Bhote Koshi floods hit, it opened the eyes of the world to the risks.

Dhakal said the Bhote Koshi floods “have proved the impacts of climate change in the Himalayan region”, which were linked to rising temperatures by scientists with the World Weather Attribution group. “Therefore, Nepal wants scientific studies, research and political discussions on mountain climate risks to receive greater attention at international climate conferences,” he added.

Nepal has been making efforts on this front since 2009, when it held a cabinet meeting at Kalapatthar near Mount Everest. Since COP28 in Dubai, Nepal has organised high-level events and dialogues on mountain issues at COPs and is co-hosting one at COP31 with Bhutan, Pakistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

Editor’s Desk: Nepal’s disaster has laid bare the world’s adaptation accountability gap

Dhakal said the dialogues held so far have raised awareness, but mountain concerns must become part of the formal UN climate process to unlock climate finance and technical support that can bolster countries’ capacity to tackle climate threats.

If specific indicators and priorities are developed for mountain regions, vulnerable developing countries like Nepal would have better access to finance to help them adapt to the climate warming they have done very little to cause, he added.

More detailed data would enable them to prepare stronger project proposals for international climate funds, including the Green Climate Fund (GCF). In 2025, the GCF backed a project to protect livelihoods from climate-induced flooding in Nepal but it took seven years to get approval.

Sindhu Dhungana, an alternate board member at the GCF, said the problem is becoming more widespread and urgent for the Hindu Kush Himalaya region.

“The economies, cultures and almost everything in Himalayan countries depend on mountains,” he explained. “For us, climate change is mountain change… [it has] affected everything, including the economy and biodiversity.”

Debris and mud cover buildings in DevGhat village in Nepal (Photo: Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images) Debris and mud cover buildings in DevGhat village in Nepal (Photo: Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images)

Destroyed development projects

Nepal wants the UN climate process to address mountain risks both before and after disasters. Countries need better research, technology, early warning systems and other adaptation measures to protect people and infrastructure. But even when countries take precautions, loss and damage is likely to occur and will require international support to address it.

Nepal has been provisionally allocated $21.6 million from the United Nations' new Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) to help with the aftermath of the Bhote Koshi disaster, but this is just a fraction of needs and the money will come only months after it made an initial request.

Dhakal pointed to the damage caused by floods to infrastructure built with loans, such as the Melamchi Drinking Water Project, which received $312 million from the Asian Development Bank but was destroyed by a major flood in 2021, shortly after it began operating. The recent Bhote Koshi disaster wiped out a dozen hydropower facilities, as well as solar energy systems.

Nepal flood destruction shows “limits to adaptation”, scientists say

Nepal wants international discussions on what should happen when climate-related disasters destroy development projects built using credit, and how the loans should be treated afterwards.

"Climatic disasters wash out… projects, but the burden of loan is still paid by Nepal," Dhakal said.

For now, it remains unclear whether the opening session of COP31 will consider or adopt the proposed agenda item on mountains and climate change, with consultations on how to respond still underway among governments and the COP31 co-presidencies.

"If countries agree to discuss the proposal and include it in the agenda, that would be another step forward," Dhakal said. "Further discussions in the coming years could gradually give the mountain agenda a stronger shape."

title: Foreign Minister Khanal leaves for Turkiye, leading Nepali Delegation to COP31 - The Rising Nepal
description: Foreign Minister Khanal leaves for Turkiye, leading Nepali Delegation to COP31  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov 7: Minister for Foreign Affairs Shisir Khanal departed for Antalya, Turkiye today, leading a Nepali delegation to the Thirty First Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).

The Conference is scheduled to be held from November 9 to 20. The Foreign Minister will address the Opening Plenary of the COP31 on November 9, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

Likewise, he will also participate in the Leader’s Summit on November 11-12.

In addition, the Foreign Minister will engage in various high-level events including ‘Advancing the Mountain Agenda: Glaciers, Cryosphere and Resilience under Overshoot, Shared Responsibility and Sustainable Financing’, jointly hosted by Nepal, Republic of Tajikistan, Kyrgyz Republic, Kingdom of Bhutan and Islamic Republic of Pakistan.

He will also participate in other side events and hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts and other dignitaries.

The delegation comprises Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Gita Chaudhary, Member of the National Planning Commission Prof. Dr Sanjaya Acharya, Secretary at the Agriculture, Forest and Environment Ministry, Dr Rajendra Prasad Mishra, and other senior government officials.

Minister Khanal will return home on November 14.

By TRN Online, Kathmandu, Nov. 7: Pakistani Ambassador to Nepal Mohammad Amir Khan has said that the future of youth is linked to startups, technology and innovation.

He believes that if young people can give a professional form to new ideas, they can create ample opportunities in their own country.

Speaking at the Startup Summit Nepal 2026 in Pokhara on Friday, Ambassador Khan said that new possibilities for entrepreneurship are expanding with the development of technology. He urged the youth to prioritize creativity, innovative thinking, and the use of technology.

Noting that Pakistan also has experience in developing startups and technology-based enterprises, he said that cooperation between Nepal and Pakistan can create new opportunities in promoting entrepreneurship.

According to him, in today's competitive world, it is not possible to advance a business solely through traditional thinking. Young entrepreneurs can create great potential if they can connect new technology and creative concepts with market needs.

title: Hester Biosciences Limited reviews Nepal after PPR shortfall - Multibagg AI
description: Hester Biosciences Limited reviews Nepal after PPR shortfall  Multibagg AI
publisher.title: Multibagg AI
full_article:
What happened to Hester's Nepal PPR procurement?

Hester said expected Nepal procurement tied to international PPR eradication programmes did not emerge at the scale it had originally envisaged. PPR is a disease-control programme context identified by management, but Hester did not quantify the opportunity, actual supplies, revenue foregone or the period in which procurement fell short.

Management's response is an assessment of how to adapt the Nepal business to the prevailing environment, rather than a disclosed exit, restructuring charge, investment commitment or revised sales forecast. Hester said it would share further developments as that assessment progresses, and listed a commercially viable Nepal path among its priorities for the remainder of FY27.

The disclosure separates Nepal from Hester's broader international operations, which management described as broadly stable in Q2 FY27. During the quarter, international supplies served tender requirements and other institutional and export orders across Asia and Africa, while Nepal was specifically identified as the market where programme-led procurement did not reach anticipated scale.

How does Nepal compare with Hester's Africa operations?

Nepal and Hester Africa face different stated priorities: Hester is assessing a viable model for Nepal after the PPR procurement shortfall, while it is seeking a more consistent business and improved financial sustainability in Africa. For both operations, management said the commercial objective is to convert product registrations and market access into orders, without providing country-level revenue or profitability for Q2 or H1 FY27.

For Hester Africa, management said an amendment to its loan agreement with the Gates Foundation had provided financial support while efforts to strengthen operating performance continued. H1 FY27 consolidated profitability included an exceptional accounting gain recognised in Q1 following that amendment, which management said contributed significantly to reported H1 profit growth and should be viewed separately from operating performance.

In the question session, management discussed financial support for the wholly owned Africa subsidiary and clarified that a 15 November date mentioned in the relevant agreement related to signing, not repayment. Rajiv Gandhi said the support was intended to fortify operations through administration and required finances, not to confirm a specific order, tender award or delivery schedule.

Management also said products manufactured at the Africa plant had been registered in several markets within Africa as well as in the Middle East and Asia. Priya Gandhi said those registrations could support entry into more markets, but gave no revenue target, order book figure or timetable for the Africa operation in H2 FY27.

title: Balen Shah's U-turn: Nepal PM meets top Indian diplomat months after snub - India Today
description: Balen Shah's U-turn: Nepal PM meets top Indian diplomat months after snub  India Today
publisher.title: India Today
full_article:
Around six months ago, Nepal Prime Minister Balen Shah refused to meet the Indian foreign secretary, which resulted in Vikram Misri's visit being postponed. Nepalese media reports then cited Shah's reluctance to meet with foreign officials who are not of an equivalent level. On Thursday, he sat down with the very same Indian diplomat. Perhaps, this time Shah's ego had to make way for pragmatism as Nepal just cannot brush away its largest trading partner.

advertisement ❮❯

Read Full Story

On Thursday, Shah met Misri in Kathmandu as the foreign secretary wrapped up his two-day visit to the Himalayan nation. It comes ahead of the Nepal PM's visit to India later this month (November 22 likely), in what will be his first bilateral trip since assuming office in March. The decision is another major turnaround by Shah, who previously decided not to make foreign visits in his first year in office. Balen Shah's visit to India later this month will be the first visit by a Nepal PM in three years (AP)Â

BALEN SHAH MEETS FOREIGN SECY

During his meeting with Misri, Shah was seen without his usual trademark sunglasses. Perhaps taking them off helped him see the importance of ties with India more clearly. The talks focused on water resources, energy, and trade, a joint statement said.

The U-turn is striking. Around six months ago, Misri had to unexpectedly call off his two-day visit to Kathmandu in May. While no reason was provided by India, a report in The Kathmandu Post cited Shah's self-imposed rule of avoiding one-on-one meetings with foreign diplomats.

The report, which quoted government officials, framed the approach as a "new protocol" where the PM won't meet officials below the foreign minister level.

It was not just Misri. Shah also refused meetings with US assistant secretary of state Paul Kapur and US envoy to India Sergio Gor earlier this year.

In the Indian context, Misri's visit was considered important to engage with the new leadership in Kathmandu after the violent Gen Z protests last year. Apart from trade and energy ties, Nepal's unique geographical position is key to India's security.

The snub to India came as the long-running border dispute over the Kalapani-Lipulekh junction resurfaced.

The tensions compounded after India and China agreed to reopen the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra via Uttarakhand's Lipulekh Pass. Kathmandu claims Lipulekh as part of its territory under the 1816 Sugauli Treaty. India rejected Nepal's position, describing its territorial claims as "untenable".

However, since then, Nepal has signalled that it was willing to address the issue diplomatically. In the background, engagements continued.

advertisement

In June, the chairperson of Balen Shah's Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), Rabi Lamichhane, received a high-profile and warm welcome in New Delhi. The next month, Shah broke his self-imposed protocol to meet Indian ambassador Naveen Srivastava.

WHAT'S BEHIND NEPAL PM'S TURNAROUND?

And then, flash floods struck Nepal. It left over 1,400 dead and 6,000 missing.

The flood, triggered by a glacial collapse in upstream Tibet, swept through parts of the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, swallowing towns, roads and bridges.

India acted swiftly to rush over hundreds of tonnes of emergency relief material and equipment like Bailey bridges to restore connectivity to far-flung areas. New Delhi also dispatched tunnelling experts and rescue teams to help workers stranded inside tunnels at hydropower projects.

According to the MEA, India rushed over 140 tonnes of relief material between August 26 and September 19, reinforcing its 'first responder' image whenever its neighbours face a crisis.

India also came in praise from Balen Shah in his first address at the UNGA in New York in September. In fact, the Nepalese PM also proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism between Nepal, India and China to tackle climate-change-related disasters.

advertisement

The tone towards India had begun to change. Experts said there is also an important economic reason for Nepal to strengthen its ties with India.

Constantino Xavier, an expert on South Asian affairs, cited an economic angle behind the sudden shift in Nepal's approach.

"Nepal and other neighbours realise rising reliance on and benefits of closer economic relations with India to attain developmental objectives - especially given global slowdown and disruptions," Xavier, a visiting professor at Ashoka University, tweeted.

To buttress his point, he shared a news report from The Kathmandu Post that said Nepal has sought an economic package worth more than $2 billion (Rs 18,786 crore), comprising lines of credit and grants, from India.

The economic package came up for discussion during the meeting between Misri and Shah, the report said. A Nepal finance ministry official said an announcement is likely to be made during Shah's visit to India. There has been no statement from New Delhi.

Nepal said the funds would primarily be used to construct transmission lines and for reconstruction efforts following the flash floods.

Professor Mushtaq Hussain, faculty (international relations) at BITS Law School, said Nepal's need for economic cooperation with India might have determined Shah's change in approach.

advertisement

"India is the largest trade partner of Nepal and a crucial transit country for its imports and exports. Nepal's economic concerns, coupled with the need to finance the reconstruction after the devastating floods, will feature prominently in Shah's visit," Hussain told IndiaToday.in.

THE GORKHA FACTOR

Crucially, Shah's move to pick India, and not China, for his first bilateral foreign visit indicates his eagerness to reshape ties with New Delhi.

Prof Hussain said Shah would definitely try to raise some of the irritants that continue to test relations. "Balen Shah's decision to choose India over China is rooted in the economic and geopolitical realities of Nepal," he said.

Apart from border issues, another key irritant has been the pause in the recruitment of Gorkha soldiers in the Indian Army following the Agnipath scheme. Under the scheme, introduced in 2022, only up to 25% of recruits would be retained for permanent service after four years.

This irked Nepal, which subsequently suspended the recruitment of Nepali youths in the Indian Army. It argued that the scheme was not in accordance with the 1947 tripartite agreement signed between India, Nepal and Britain.

However, earlier this week, India revamped the scheme to allow Agniveers undergoing training in the three services to join the forces as regular soldiers.

advertisement

This is likely to create a more favourable environment for discussions on resuming the recruitment of Nepali Gorkhas. Coincidentally, the government move comes ahead of Balen Shah's visit.

For India, Nepal is a crucial piece in the regional security map. This is undeniable.

Five states - Bengal, Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar and Sikkim - share borders with Nepal. These are close to areas where Indian and Chinese interests overlap. Thus, for New Delhi, a Nepal that drifts too close to China will ring alarm bells.

For now, all eyes will be on Balen Shah's upcoming visit to New Delhi later this month. It will be the first visit by a Nepali PM in three years. The last visit happened in 2023, when then Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal travelled to New Delhi.

title: Nepal issues new standards for managing altitude sickness in high mountain areas - The Tourism Times
description: Nepal issues new standards for managing altitude sickness in high mountain areas  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: The Ministry of Health and Population has issued new standards for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of altitude sickness in high-altitude and Himalayan areas, including provisions for emergency evacuation, referral and the supply of essential medicines and equipment.

The ‘Standards for Management of High Altitude Mountain Sickness, 2083’ have been issued under the Public Health Service Act, 2075, with the aim of improving health services for people travelling, trekking and mountaineering in high mountain areas.

The standards classify altitude sickness into three categories: acute mountain sickness (AMS), high-altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE) and high-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE). AMS may develop within eight to 48 hours after ascending and can cause headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, fatigue, weakness, disturbed sleep and breathing difficulties.

HAPE is described as a severe condition involving fluid accumulation in the lungs, with symptoms including breathlessness even at rest, chest heaviness, persistent coughing, frothy or blood-stained sputum, bluish skin and weakness. HACE involves swelling of the brain and may cause severe headache, loss of balance, slurred speech, confusion and loss of consciousness.

The standards recommend gradual ascent above 2,500 metres, limiting the increase in sleeping altitude to 300–500 metres per day. Travellers are advised to spend two nights at a location after every 1,000 metres of ascent, while following the ‘climb high, sleep low’ approach where possible.

Travellers are also advised to drink three to four litres of water or other fluids a day, eat carbohydrate-rich food and avoid alcohol, cigarettes and other tobacco products at high altitude. Anyone experiencing symptoms of altitude sickness should inform their companions and avoid ascending further.

For patients whose symptoms do not improve with rest, the standards recommend descending immediately by 500–1,000 metres. Oxygen, where available, and a Gamow bag or portable hyperbaric chamber may also be used. The standards state that descent is the most effective treatment for altitude sickness.

For AMS, the standards list rest, acetazolamide and stopping further ascent. For HAPE, they recommend oxygen, nifedipine, a Gamow bag, descent and immediate evacuation. HACE requires oxygen, dexamethasone, a Gamow bag, descent and urgent evacuation.

The standards also require health facilities in high mountain areas to maintain oxygen cylinders or concentrators, Gamow bags, pulse oximeters, blood-pressure equipment, stethoscopes, thermometers, nebulisers, ECG machines and emergency medical supplies.

Medicines listed include acetazolamide, dexamethasone and nifedipine, among other emergency drugs.

Under the standards, federal authorities are responsible for policy, standards, regulation, staffing and budget support, while provincial governments are tasked with training and technical support. Local governments must ensure access to designated and emergency health services, maintain supplies of medicines and equipment, and operate referral systems.

The standards are intended to improve preparedness and treatment at health facilities serving high-altitude travellers and ensure quicker evacuation and referral of serious cases.

title: Nepal Investigates Deadly Helicopter Crash Near Mount Everest - Travel Radar
description: Nepal Investigates Deadly Helicopter Crash Near Mount Everest  Travel Radar
publisher.title: Travel Radar
full_article:
One tourist was killed and three others injured in a helicopter crash in Nepal’s Everest region after two aircraft collided during an attempt to land on Nov. 3. The accident has raised concerns about aviation safety in the area, while authorities investigate the circumstances surrounding the collision.

Summary Helicopter crash kills one near EverestInvestigation into Nepal helicopter crashConcerns over helicopter safety in Nepal’s mountains

A helicopter collision in Pheriche, Nepal, on Nov. 3, killed one tourist and injured three others © Nepal Police via Reuters

Helicopter crash kills one near Everest

One tourist was killed and three injured after two helicopters collided on Tuesday, Nov. 3, while trying to land near Mount Everest base camp in Nepal.

The accident occurred at approximately 8:12 a.m. local time in Pheriche, a village in the Solukhumbu district situated at around 4,371 metres (14,341 feet) above sea level. The aircraft were operated by two private companies, Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, and collided while approaching the same landing area.

The deceased was identified as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu, an Indian national travelling aboard the Fishtail Air helicopter. The injured included a passenger from New Zealand and the pilots of both aircraft. The passenger and Fishtail Air pilot were transported to Kathmandu for treatment, while the Air Dynasty pilot received medical care in Lukla.

This comes during Nepal ’ s peak tourist season. Pheriche is a popular stop off point during the Everest Base Camp trek with helicopters providing transport .

Nepal’s Civil Aviation Authority (CAAN) investigates the cause of the fatal helicopter collision © Nepal Police via Reuters

Investigation into Nepal helicopter crash

The Air Dynasty helicopter, registered as 9N‑AOD, had been flying a cargo mission from Lukla Airport. The Fishtail Air helicopter, registered as 9N‑AJR, had landed from Gorakshep and was carrying two foreign tourists. Both aircraft were Airbus AS350 helicopters.

Video footage revealed the helicopters ’ rotors collided just before they crashed. The collision happened when the helicopters were around two to three metres from the ground as they approached the landing area from opposite directions.

Nepal ’ s Civil Aviation Authority (CAAN) has launched an investigation and set up a five- person committee comprising pilots and aircraft engineers to look into what led to the crash .

According to CAAN Director General Mukesh Dangol, initial reports suggest there may have been a lack of communication between the pilots. He explained that the accident site falls outside the coverage of Lukla Airport’s (LUA) air traffic control tower, requiring pilots operating in the area to communicate directly with one another.

The exact circumstances surrounding the collision remain under investigation, and authorities have yet to establish its definitive cause.

The latest crash has renewed concerns over helicopter safety and flight coordination in Nepal’s mountainous regions © Babin Dulal

Concerns over helicopter safety in Nepal ’ s mountains

Nepal’s mountainous regions have experienced fatal helicopter accidents in the past. In July 2023, a Manang Air helicopter crashed in the Lamjura area of Solukhumbu district, killing all six people on board. This included five Mexican nationals and one Nepali pilot.

Despite the risks, helicopters remain essential to Nepal’s mountain tourism industry. They provide transport for goods , support during mountain expeditions and can provide emergency evacuations for trekkers and climbers suffering from altitude sickness, injuries or exhaustion.

An increase in sightseeing flights has drawn complaints from local communities and conservationists over noise pollution.

In December 2024, local authorities and Sagarmatha National Park officials issued a directive seeking to restrict commercial helicopter flights in the Everest region from Jan. 1, 2025. However, the park later reversed its decision, allowing flights to operate under certain conditions, highlighting disagreements over the regulation of helicopter activity in the area.

The investigation will look into what happened during the collision and what could have contributed to it . This may offer more insight into how pilots communicate , land and manage air traffic in the Everest region.

Bangladesh Embassy, Kathmandu on Saturday observed the National Revolution and Solidarity Day in a solemn and befitting manner on the Embassy premises. Then it was followed by a program in the Embassy auditorium, including playing national anthems of Bangladesh and Nepal, remarks by speakers, special prayers seeking salvation of the martyrs, continued peace and prosperity of the country.

Messages from the President and Prime Minister of Bangladesh on the occasion of the day were read out. Two documentaries highlighting the historical background and significance of the day were also screened. During the discussion session, the speakers reflected on the historical significance of November 7 and its contribution to the nation-building process and the political history of Bangladesh. They recalled the role of Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman in restoring multiparty democracy, freedom of expression and the press and highlighted his critical role in preserving the national unity, sovereignty and people's collective aspirations in safeguarding the country's independence and democratic journey.

At least 1,400 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing.

It was the latest in a series of natural disasters that have battered Nepal in recent years as climate change accelerates.
